title: West and Central Asia, 500 BCE–1980 CE

guide.summary: This content area spans ancient Nabataean and Buddhist works to centuries of Islamic architecture and the arts of the book and loom. Recurring themes include sacred space and pilgrimage, the role of calligraphy and geometric ornament in religious contexts, the vibrant figural traditions of court manuscripts, and the exchange of ideas along trade routes.

sections.heading: Before Islam and Buddhist Central Asia
sections.body:
At **Petra** (Jordan), the Nabataeans carved the **Treasury (al-Khazneh)** directly into rose-colored sandstone cliffs, combining local traditions with Hellenistic columns and pediments, evidence of their role in long-distance trade.

The colossal **Buddhas of Bamiyan** (Afghanistan), carved into cliffs along Silk Road routes and once painted, marked a major Buddhist monastic center. The Taliban destroyed them in 2001, making them a symbol of cultural heritage under threat.

The **Jowo Rinpoche**, a gilded Buddha image in the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa, Tibet, is among the most revered Buddhist images; pilgrims make offerings, and the statue is adorned with jewels and robes.

sections.heading: Sacred architecture in Islam
sections.body:
The **Kaaba** in Mecca is Islam's holiest site, the direction of prayer (**qibla**) and focus of the **Hajj** pilgrimage. It's covered by the **kiswa**, a black textile embroidered with Qur'anic text in gold, replaced annually.

The **Dome of the Rock** in Jerusalem (691–692, Umayyad) is the earliest surviving major Islamic monument: an octagonal shrine with a gilded dome built over a rock sacred to Jews, Christians, and Muslims. Its Qur'anic inscriptions assert Islamic teachings, partly addressing the city's Christian population.

The **Great Mosque (Masjid-e Jameh) of Isfahan** grew over centuries, adding a **four-iwan plan** (large vaulted halls opening onto a courtyard) under the Seljuks and **muqarnas** vaults and tile work later.

sections.heading: Arts of the book and luxury objects
sections.body:
Islamic religious art generally avoids figural imagery (**aniconism**), emphasizing calligraphy, geometry, and vegetal patterns (arabesque). A **folio from an early Qur'an** in angular **Kufic script** on parchment shows calligraphy itself as sacred art.

Secular court arts often embraced figures. Persian manuscripts of the **Shahnama** (Book of Kings) illustrate epic stories: **Bahram Gur Fights the Karg** comes from the Great Mongol Shahnama, made for Ilkhanid Mongol rulers adopting Persian kingship traditions. **The Court of Gayumars** by Sultan Muhammad, from the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp (Safavid), is famous for minute, jewel-like detail.

The Mamluk brass **Basin (Baptistère de Saint Louis)**, inlaid with silver and gold, later baptized French royal children, showing how objects moved across cultures. The Safavid **Ardabil Carpet** (1539–1540), made for a dynastic shrine, has a central medallion with hanging lamps and an inscription naming its maker.

sections.heading: Comparing works across the region
sections.body: Compare the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (691–92), an early Islamic shrine with an octagonal plan, a golden dome, and rich mosaics with Arabic inscriptions, with the Great Mosque of Isfahan, whose four-iwan plan and muqarnas vaults developed over centuries. Both show the importance of calligraphy and geometric and vegetal ornament in Islamic art, reflecting the avoidance of figural imagery in religious contexts. The Bamiyan Buddhas, carved into cliffs in Afghanistan, show Buddhist art along Silk Road trade routes before their destruction in 2001.

sections.heading: Exam connection
sections.body: Questions often ask about the function of mosques, the role of calligraphy, or how works reflect exchange among cultures. Name architectural features precisely: mihrab, qibla wall, minaret, iwan, and courtyard.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know mihrab, qibla, minbar, minaret, iwan, muqarnas, calligraphy, arabesque, and illuminated manuscript.

sections.heading: Attribution practice
sections.body: When attributing an unfamiliar work from West or Central Asia, look for calligraphy, geometric and vegetal patterns, muqarnas, or manuscript conventions such as flattened space and detailed borders. Compare with required works like the Great Mosque of Isfahan or the Shahnama manuscript, and explain how features indicate an Islamic context.

sections.heading: Manuscripts and luxury objects
sections.body: Illuminated manuscripts, such as the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, were produced by teams of artists in royal workshops and combined calligraphy, painting, and decorative borders. Luxury objects such as ivory boxes, inlaid metalwork, and textiles circulated among courts as diplomatic gifts and displays of wealth, carrying artistic motifs across regions.

sections.heading: Essay tip
sections.body: In essays about sacred spaces, describe how worshippers move through and use the building, such as orienting prayer toward the qibla wall, and connect architectural features to religious practice. Name the work, location, and date to anchor every claim in specific evidence.

keyTakeaways: Petra and Bamiyan reflect trade-route exchange; Bamiyan's destruction raises heritage questions.
The Kaaba and Dome of the Rock define Islamic sacred space and early Islamic identity.
Religious Islamic art favors calligraphy and geometry; court manuscripts embrace figures.
Mosque architecture evolved: hypostyle halls, four-iwan plans, muqarnas.
Luxury objects traveled and gained new meanings in new contexts.
Patronage by rulers (Ilkhanid, Safavid) shaped manuscript and textile arts.
commonMistakes: Claiming all Islamic art forbids figures.
Confusing the Dome of the Rock (shrine) with a congregational mosque.
Forgetting the Bamiyan Buddhas were destroyed in 2001.
Mixing up Safavid (Ardabil Carpet, Court of Gayumars) and Mamluk (Baptistère) works.
Ignoring how objects' meanings change as they move.
examTips: Distinguish religious from secular contexts when discussing figural imagery.
Use architectural terms precisely: iwan, muqarnas, qibla, mihrab, hypostyle.
Continuity-and-change questions fit Isfahan's long building history well.
Patrons and dynasties matter; name them.
Note materials: gold-inlaid brass, wool and silk carpets, parchment.

distractors.C: No such prohibition exists, and Petra predates Islam.

practice.stimulus: A mosque in Iran was built over many centuries. Its courtyard is framed by four large vaulted halls, one on each side, and several have ceilings made of tiers of small niches resembling honeycomb.

practice.stimulus: A horizontal parchment page from an early Qur'an contains a few lines of angular, elongated Arabic script in brown ink, with gold ornaments marking verse divisions. There are no figures.
practice.stem: Which statement best explains the page's design?

choices.text: The page was a Christian manuscript.
The scribe lacked the skill to paint figures.
The page was a draft for a Persian epic.
In a religious text, calligraphy itself conveys sacred beauty, consistent with aniconism in Islamic religious art.

practice.explanation: Kufic calligraphy elevates the word of God; figural images were avoided in sacred texts.

distractors.B: Islamic artists produced elaborate figural art in secular contexts.

that the basin was originally made for Christian baptism

practice.stem: Which statement best explains why figural imagery is common in Persian Shahnama manuscripts but absent from early Qur'an pages?

practice.explanation: Context determines conventions; aniconism applies mainly to religious settings.

practice.stimulus: A late seventh-century shrine in Jerusalem is decorated with mosaics of vegetal forms and crowns, and with Qur'anic inscriptions, including passages about the nature of Jesus in Islamic teaching.

To convert the shrine into a church

distractors.B: It was built as an Islamic shrine.

practice.stem: Which factor best explains why monumental Buddhist sculptures were carved at Bamiyan?

choices.text: The sculptures were carved in the twentieth century as tourist attractions.
Bamiyan was the capital of the Roman Empire.
The site was chosen to face Mecca.

practice.explanation: Trade wealth and the movement of monks and pilgrims made Bamiyan a major Buddhist center.

distractors.C: They predate Islam in the region.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe ONE architectural feature added to the mosque under the Seljuks.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe ONE way the mosque maintained continuity with earlier mosque traditions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how later additions changed the experience of the mosque. Use specific evidence.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why a congregational mosque might be modified by successive rulers over centuries.

rubric.description: The four-iwan plan around the courtyard, or brick domes over the prayer hall.
E.g., the central courtyard, hypostyle prayer halls, orientation toward the qibla with a mihrab.
E.g., muqarnas vaults create complex, shimmering transitions between spaces.
E.g., later glazed tile revetment added color and calligraphy, transforming surfaces.
Rulers sponsored additions to demonstrate piety and power, associate themselves with an important religious center, and meet the needs of a growing community.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Under the Seljuks, the mosque was reorganized around a four-iwan plan, with a large vaulted hall opening onto each side of the courtyard.

(b) The mosque kept the central courtyard and columned prayer halls of earlier congregational mosques, and remained oriented toward the qibla, with a mihrab marking the direction of Mecca.

(c) Later builders added muqarnas vaults inside the iwans, whose honeycomb niches break up surfaces so that light seems to flicker, making transitions between spaces dramatic. Glazed tile with geometric patterns and calligraphy was added over the brick, giving the courtyard vivid color and inscriptions that reinforce its religious message.

(d) Sponsoring additions to the main mosque of a major city allowed each ruler to demonstrate piety and political authority in a highly visible place, while also enlarging and updating a building used by the whole community for Friday prayers.
